newsitem.title: USA: Republicans vow to kill arts funding.
newsitem.headline: Republicans vow to kill arts funding.

text.p: House Republican Leader Dick Armey vowed Tuesday his party would kill the National Endowment for the Arts this year, calling it an elitist organisation that acted as a cultural censor.
Waving a dollar bill during testimony to a House hearing, Armey said he was willing to support the arts out of his own pocket, but said it was time to quit coercing taxpayer support for the NEA.

"It flies in the face of freedom and it smacks at the outset of censorship," said the Texas Republican, adding he was "deeply, deeply offended" by the suggestion federal money was needed for the arts to flourish in the United States.
Later Tuesday, conservative and religious groups announced they were forming a coalition to push Congress to defund the NEA, charging it was promoting immoral works.

"I hope that the Republican leadership has the courage and the wit to eliminate funding for the NEA," former education secretary William Bennett said in a statement. "Beating a retreat from such obviously favourable political terrain paves the way for further demoralisation and surrender."
But behind the bluster was the sense Republicans may not have the votes to make good on their promise.
Under pressure from conservatives in their party, House Republican leaders have promised they will not let any bill through the chamber that continues funding for the NEA.
They admit privately they likely do not have the votes in either congressional chamber to block the NEA for good.
Some Republicans challenged Armey's testimony at the hearing, offering their own testimonials in support of the NEA which will receive about $100 million in funds this year.
NEA Chairman Jane Alexander defended her agency, saying it had made art accessible across the nation, with funding amounting to less than 38 cents from each American.
"Will we be the only major nation on earth to deny a federal role in our country's artistic endeavours?" she said.
Missouri Democrat William Clay challenged Armey, holding up a $20 bill and complaining that the bulk of that money would be used by Congress to support the military and other programmes.
"There is something wrong with our priorities when we want to spend nothing on the cultural activities of this nation and an excessive amount on arms," Clay said.
Armey joked he initially thought Clay planned to contribute the $20 to the NEA, in which case he wouldn't be a liberal, "it being your own money."
